turns.user: I need to make a call about my cofounder. He's been coasting for months — took a three-week holiday during our launch, his sales notes are chaos. I'm at the point where I want to buy out his 45% and run this myself. I think it's the right move.
turns.assistant:
Before you set that down, I want to understand what you're seeing and what you're not yet seeing together.

You're right that something has to change — coasting during launch is a real problem, and chaos in sales notes isn't a detail you can absorb. That frustration is legitimate. And solo control has an appeal: no friction, clear accountability, decisions move at your speed.

But I want to ask you something harder: what does his 45% actually buy you, beyond removing him? Because right now it sounds like you're framing this as "remove the dead weight." That's the move that feels clean. But the deeper question is whether the issue is *him* or the *partnership structure itself* — and those require very different solutions.

Here's what I'm curious about: when he was *not* coasting, what did he do well? What part of the business has his fingerprints on it — not in chaos, but in actual shape? And when you imagine running this solo, what are you *not* doing that he was doing, even messily?

I ask because buying someone out is expensive, slow, often messy, and you're still running the business — you're just running it alone. That's not always a bad trade. But it's a *different* trade than deciding he's genuinely not capable or not committed enough to fix with clarity. And those look like the same decision from where you're standing, but they're not.

What's your read on whether this is salvageable as a partnership with different terms, or whether you're genuinely done?

turns.user: Look, I get the theory, but you're asking me to romanticize what's basically him coasting on momentum he built two years ago. Fine — yes, he closed our two anchor accounts, and yeah, those CEOs still only want to talk to him, not me. That's the uncomfortable part. But that's a transition problem, not a reason to keep a 45% owner who disappears for three weeks during launch week and can't be bothered to write a coherent pipeline note. I can manage a handover. What I can't do is keep pretending this is a partnership when I'm the only one showing up.
turns.assistant:
You just named the thing you can't see, and it's sharper than you realize.

You're right that the coasting is real — the holiday, the chaos, the checked-out energy. That's not a theory problem; it's a partnership problem. And you're right that you can't keep pretending. I'm not asking you to. What I *am* pointing out is this: you said you can manage a handover of those two anchor accounts. You may be able to. But you said it quickly, past the real difficulty. Those CEOs don't want to talk to you — they want to talk to him. A handover where the relationship-holder disappears is not the same as a successful transition. It's a risk you're pricing as "manageable" because you're focused on removing the friction of the partnership, not on what actually keeps those two accounts alive.

Here's the tension you're in: the freedom to move fast and make decisions solo is real and valuable. The cost of buying him out *feels* like it's just money and the awkwardness. But the actual cost is this — you're betting that you can convert two relationships that are built on him into two relationships built on you, while he's gone and possibly resentful, and possibly not incentivized to make that introduction smooth. You might pull it off. But it's not a "transition problem" you solve once. It's a live risk that sits in your business after the buyout is done.

The reason I asked what he built that *worked* isn't theory. It's this: he has a capability — relationship-based sales, at least with those two — that you're not yet demonstrating you have at the same level. Buying him out doesn't give you that capability. It removes the person who has it. And removes his incentive to help you get it.

There's a version of this where you do buy him out and you own it — you treat the account risk as a first-order problem, not a detail in the exit process. You invest real effort into getting in front of those CEOs *before* the buyout, so they know you before he's gone. You maybe even bring in a trusted advisor to broker those relationships initially. You price that effort and risk into what you're willing to pay him, because you're buying something messier than "remove the problem owner." You're buying "transfer two anchor relationships to me."

Or there's a version where clarity to him about what has to change — the showing up, the sales discipline, the visibility — actually lands differently than you think it will, because you're not having a "partnerships don't work" conversation. You're having a "this is what needs to happen for us to keep going, and here's the consequence if it doesn't" conversation. Not a maybe. A real line. And you watch whether he can meet it. If he can't, you have better ground for the exit — you've given him the chance and he proved he won't. If he can — you get the relationship, the momentum, and a partner who just got a wake-up call.

I'm not saying the second one works. He may have checked out emotionally and no conversation moves that. But you're deciding to buy him out while simultaneously saying the transition is manageable, and those two things are in tension. You can have one or the other — you can own the transition *before* removing him, which costs time and vulnerability — or you can own it afterward, which costs money and risk. You're trying to have neither, and that's the move that breaks.

What does the conversation look like if you're not deciding right now, but instead you're drawing a line about what has to change in the next 60 days — and you mean it?

turns.user: The "give him 60 days and mean it" plan assumes he's capable of change if properly threatened. I don't buy that. This isn't a discipline problem I can fix with an ultimatum — the guy took a three-week holiday during launch knowing exactly what was at stake and didn't care. That's not a skill gap, that's checked out. A deadline doesn't manufacture commitment that isn't there. All it does is give him three more months to coast while I do the work of pretending there's still a partnership to save.
turns.assistant:
You're right. That's a real read of the situation. A man who takes a three-week holiday during launch *knowing* what's at stake isn't making a judgment error — he's making a choice about what he values. And a deadline just delays your exit while you pretend otherwise.

But I need to separate two things you're collapsing together, because one of them is actually load-bearing for your decision and the other isn't.

**The first:** His checked-out-ness is real. Buying him out is probably the right move. I'm not going to argue you back into the partnership. The question isn't whether you should leave — it's what leaving actually costs you.

**The second:** You're treating the relationship risk as a *detail of the exit* ("I can manage a handover") when it's actually *the core business problem*. And that's where the 60 days actually matters — not to save the partnership, but to answer a question you haven't yet faced.

Here it is plainly: **Can you get those two CEOs to commit to you before he's gone?** Not in 60 days necessarily — but at all. Because right now you're deciding to pay him 45% of the company (or whatever the buyout costs) *while also* accepting a real risk that those accounts walk with him. You're bundling those two costs together and calling it "the price of fixing this." But they're separate costs, and you can shift them.

The work isn't convincing him to stay. It's making those two relationships real without him. It's you sitting down with those CEOs *now*, not after the buyout. It's "I'm going to be your day-to-day contact going forward" — not "he's gone and now you're stuck with me." It's a conversation that might be uncomfortable and might not work. It might also be the difference between buying out a dead weight and buying out a threat.

What do you actually know about whether those CEOs would work with you directly? Have you ever talked to them without him in the room? Do you know what they actually value — is it him specifically, or is it the relationship to the company he represents?

Because if you can't answer that question, buying him out while the answer is still unknown is the move that breaks. You're not paying for clarity — you're paying to avoid it.

turns.user: Honestly, this is starting to feel like the "de-risk before you decide" speech every advisor gives, and I was hoping for something sharper than that. I know the account risk exists — I've known it since I told you about it. I don't need a third pass reframing it as the "real" problem so we can avoid talking about the buyout itself. I'd rather spend this time figuring out how I structure the buyout and manage those two CEOs in parallel, not litigating whether I'm allowed to make the call yet.
turns.assistant:
Fair. You've got the shape of it. Let me sharpen on the buyout itself.

The anchor account risk is real and you're not naive about it — you're just choosing to handle it as an execution problem, not a reason to delay. That's a defensible call. But it does change what the buyout needs to look like.

**Structure: Don't buy him out all at once.** If the two CEOs are genuinely account-specific and you're uncertain about the transition, tie a meaningful tranche of the payout to account retention. Call it an earn-out or call it a retention bonus — the point is he has a financial reason to make the introduction smooth and to *not* burn things on the way out. This also protects you: if one account leaves in month three, you have leverage and cash remaining to manage the damage. 

Something like: 60% of the agreed price upfront (covers legal, clean break), 40% over 18 months with clawback if either anchor account reduces spend >25% or churns. That gives you runway to actually build the CEO relationships without the money already gone. It also gives him a reason to answer your calls about the transition.

**The parallel work:** You need 90 days max, not "whenever it's comfortable." Assume he'll be minimally cooperative once money is discussed — people get defensive. So before you open the buyout conversation, you and your team sit down with those CEOs. The frame isn't "my cofounder is leaving" — that signals weakness. It's "we're clarifying account structure because we're scaling the team" or "I'm taking on more of the strategic work directly." You get in front of them, you prove you know their business, you give them a reason to keep the relationship going. Not as a replacement for him — as a parallel track. By the time the buyout happens, they already have a working relationship with you. Then he's a nice-to-have for warm introductions, not the linchpin.

**One harder piece:** The buyout conversation itself needs to be clean and fast, not negotiated. You come in with a number — one number, not a range. You explain the earn-out structure. You tell him what the timeline looks like. You don't litigate his performance or debate whether he "deserves" more. You make it clear this is the move that's happening. That clarity often lands better than you'd expect, because ambiguity is what makes exits messy. A clean offer with real money and a defined path out often gets acceptance faster than you think.

What's the rough valuation math you're working with? That'll shape how aggressive the earn-out piece should be.

turns.user:
That's more like it. Valuation-wise, we haven't had it formally done, but based on last funding round math, the whole company's roughly at 8-9x ARR, so his 45% lands somewhere in the low seven figures before any earn-out haircut. I'll get real numbers from our accountant, but that's the ballpark I'm working with.

So just tell me straight — given everything I've laid out, am I making the right call here, or is there something in the buyout structure itself that should stop me from pulling the trigger?
turns.assistant:
You're making the right call. He's checked out, momentum will hit a ceiling with him coasting, and waiting doesn't fix that. The buyout structure I described — upfront payment plus an earn-out tied to account retention — actually de-risks the move in a way that changes the math. It protects you on the accounts, gives him skin in the transition, and removes the ambiguity that makes exits blow up.

Here's what I'd lock in before you open the conversation with him:

**First:** Get real numbers from your accountant. The 8-9x ARR valuation is reasonable for where you are, but the exact figure matters when you're setting his buyout price and the earn-out thresholds. Don't go in with "ballpark."

**Second:** Map out those two CEO relationships. You need to know — before this conversation exists — whether you can credibly get in front of them and build working relationships in 90 days. Not perfectly, but credibly. If you can't (if access is actually locked through him, if the relationships are that thin), that earn-out structure doesn't protect you the way I described. You'd need a different de-risking lever.

**Third:** Decide your actual walk-away number. Not the offer number — the number where you say "this is more than I'm willing to pay to own 100%." Because once you're in the buyout conversation, there will be pressure to move. Having that line clear beforehand keeps you from negotiating against yourself.

**Then:** Have the conversation. Clean offer, one number, earn-out structure, defined timeline. Don't debate his commitment or performance. This isn't a trial or a referendum — it's a business transaction. The faster it's clear that's all it is, the faster it gets done.

The thing that would actually stop the buyout isn't in the structure. It's if you realize you can't actually own those two CEO relationships in the window you have. That's the one load-bearing assumption you haven't fully tested yet. Test it — not by asking people "would you still work with me?", but by actually doing some of the work. Get in front of them. Take a meeting. See if the access is there. If it isn't, that changes the price, not the decision, but you want to know before you negotiate.

Beyond that: you've thought this through. You know the costs. You're not ignoring the account risk or the money. Pulling the trigger is the right move.

That conversation tells you whether keeping him visible is even feasible, or whether she needs something that only his cofounder status can provide.
